questions.stem: A student investigates how the length of a pendulum affects its period, keeping the mass of the bob and the release angle the same. What is the independent variable?
options: The release angle
The length of the pendulum
The period of the pendulum
The mass of the bob
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one the experimenter deliberately changes, here the length. The period is measured in response, so it is the dependent variable. The mass and release angle are held constant, so they are controlled variables.

questions.stem: A student investigates how the launch angle of a projectile launcher affects the range, using the same ball and the same launch speed every time. Which are controlled variables?
options: The range and the launch speed
The launch angle and the ball used
The ball used and the launch speed
The launch angle and the range
questions.explanation: Controlled variables are kept the same so that only the independent variable, the launch angle, can affect the dependent variable, the range. Here the ball and the launch speed are held constant.

questions.stem: Which is a well-written hypothesis for an investigation of a magnet falling through copper tubes of different wall thickness?
options: Copper tubes of five wall thicknesses, all 1.0 m long, will be used with the same magnet in each trial
The magnet will fall more slowly in some tubes than in others, depending on several factors
If wall thickness increases, the fall time will increase, as larger induced currents oppose the motion
What is the effect of the wall thickness of a copper tube on the time a magnet takes to fall?
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable prediction that links the independent and dependent variables and gives a reason based on physics. The question form is a research question, the list of tubes is part of a method, and the vague prediction cannot be tested because it names no relationship.

questions.stem: The VCE physics investigation must have one continuous independent variable. Which of these is continuous?
options: The current in a coil, measured in amperes
The type of metal used to make the wire
The brand of battery used in the circuit
Which pole of the magnet faces the coil
questions.explanation: A continuous variable can take any value within a range, such as a current of 0.25 A or 0.26 A. The type of metal, the brand of battery and the pole facing the coil are categories, which cannot be graphed as a continuous relationship.

questions.stem: A student uses computer software to compare satellite orbits at different radii, because real satellites cannot be manipulated. Which investigation methodology is this?
options: Literature review
Simulation
Fieldwork
Case study
questions.explanation: A simulation uses a model to study a system whose variables cannot be controlled directly, often because it is too large, too distant or too dangerous. A literature review collates other people’s findings rather than generating data from a model.

questions.stem: Sorting stars into groups by the features of their spectra is an example of which investigation methodology?
options: Case study
Classification and identification
Simulation
Product, process or system development
questions.explanation: Classification arranges objects or events into sets, and identification recognises which set something belongs to. The study design gives the classification of stars in astrophysics as a typical example.

questions.stem: What does the accuracy of a measurement describe?
options: The smallest change an instrument can detect
Whether the method measures what it is meant to
How close it is to the true value
How close repeated measurements are to each other
questions.explanation: Accuracy is closeness to the true value. Closeness of repeated measurements to each other is precision, the smallest detectable change is resolution, and measuring what was intended is validity.

questions.stem: Five measurements of g are 9.62, 9.63, 9.61, 9.62 and 9.63 m s⁻². The accepted value is 9.80 m s⁻². How should these results be described?
options: Accurate but not precise
Both accurate and precise
Neither accurate nor precise
Precise but not accurate
questions.explanation: The results agree closely with one another, so they are precise, but they are all well below the accepted value, so they are not accurate. A consistent offset like this suggests a systematic error.

questions.stem: A digital multimeter displays voltage to the nearest 0.01 V. Which property of the instrument does this describe?
options: Resolution
Accuracy
Validity
Reproducibility
questions.explanation: Resolution is the smallest change in a quantity that an instrument can detect, here 0.01 V. A meter can show many decimal places and still be inaccurate if it is badly calibrated, so the display does not tell you its accuracy.

questions.stem: A student in another school follows the same method with different equipment and gets results very close to the original student’s. This shows that the results are:
options: reproducible
repeatable but not reproducible
accurate
valid
questions.explanation: Reproducibility is agreement when the investigation is done by different people, with different equipment or in a different place. Repeatability is agreement when the same person repeats it under the same conditions. Agreement alone does not prove accuracy, as both could share the same error.

questions.stem: A student investigating how wire length affects resistance leaves the current on for longer in each trial, so the wire gets hotter in later trials. What does this mainly threaten?
options: Resolution, because the ohmmeter reads to only one decimal place
Reproducibility, because other students would use a different wire
Precision only, because heating is a type of random error
Validity, because temperature has become an uncontrolled variable
questions.explanation: Resistance depends on temperature, so the results now reflect changes in both length and temperature, and the experiment no longer tests only the effect of length. That makes it invalid. Steadily rising temperature is a systematic effect, not a random one.

questions.stem: The zero end of a metre ruler has worn away, so every length measured from that end reads 5 mm too long. What kind of error is this?
options: A random error, which reduces precision
A random error, which averaging will remove
A personal error, which repeating will remove
A systematic error, which reduces accuracy
questions.explanation: An error that shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction is systematic. It reduces accuracy and is not removed by repeating or averaging, because every repeat has the same offset. It is found by calibrating against a known standard.

questions.stem: How can the effect of random errors on a measured pendulum period best be reduced?
options: Use a heavier bob so that the pendulum swings more slowly
Keep only the result that is closest to the expected value
Time ten swings several times and average the results
Recalibrate the stopwatch against a known time standard
questions.explanation: Random errors scatter results unpredictably above and below the true value, so timing many swings and averaging repeated trials reduces their effect. Calibration corrects systematic errors. Keeping only the expected result is selective reporting, which is unethical.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes error from uncertainty?
options: Error and uncertainty mean the same thing, but error is in units and uncertainty is in percent
Error is the difference from the true value; uncertainty is the range in which the true value is likely to lie
Error is caused only by mistakes; uncertainty is caused only by faulty instruments that need repair
Error can always be removed by repeating; uncertainty can only be removed by better instruments
questions.explanation: Error is how far a measured value is from the true value, and it can be random or systematic. Uncertainty describes the doubt in a result, given as a range such as ± 0.02 s. Mistakes are not counted as errors at all; they are avoided or the measurement is repeated.

questions.stem: A student misreads a stopwatch and records 25.3 s instead of 2.53 s for one trial. How should this be treated?
options: As a mistake, which should be identified and the trial repeated
As a random error, which averaging with other trials will reduce
As a systematic error, corrected by subtracting 22.8 s from it
As an uncertainty, shown by adding an uncertainty bar to the graph
questions.explanation: Misreading an instrument is a mistake, not an error in the scientific sense. It should be identified, noted in the logbook and the trial repeated. Averaging it in would distort the mean, and it does not affect every reading the way a systematic error does.

questions.stem: Five trials of a trolley’s speed give 1.21, 1.19, 1.22, 1.58 and 1.20 m s⁻¹. How should the 1.58 m s⁻¹ result be treated?
options: Include it in the mean, because every trial must always be averaged together
Replace it with 1.20 m s⁻¹ so that the set of results looks more consistent
Note it in the logbook as an outlier and exclude it from the mean, giving a reason
Erase it from the logbook so that it cannot affect the final mean value at all
questions.explanation: 1.58 m s⁻¹ is far from the other four, so it is an outlier. It should be recorded, investigated for a cause and, if excluded from the mean, the reason stated. Erasing or altering data breaches ethical conduct and the logbook’s role in authenticating results.

questions.stem: A length is measured as 0.250 ± 0.005 m. What is the percentage uncertainty?
questions.explanation: Percentage uncertainty = (uncertainty/value) × 100 = (0.005/0.250) × 100 = 2.0%. Treating the absolute uncertainty of 0.005 as a fraction gives 0.50%, which forgets to divide by the measured value.

questions.stem: Repeated measurements of a period are 1.42, 1.46, 1.44, 1.40 and 1.48 s. Taking the uncertainty as half the range, how should the result be reported?
questions.explanation: The mean is 7.20/5 = 1.44 s. The range is 1.48 − 1.40 = 0.08 s, and half of that gives an uncertainty of ± 0.04 s. Using the whole range doubles the uncertainty.

questions.stem: A student times a ball falling 1.0 m with a hand-held stopwatch, and the times are widely scattered. Which change would most improve the precision of the timing?
options: Use light gates connected to a data logger to time the fall
Use a heavier ball, so that the ball falls a little faster
Round each of the times to fewer decimal places
Take one very careful measurement instead of five
questions.explanation: The scatter comes mainly from human reaction time in starting and stopping the watch. Light gates remove that source of random error, so repeated times agree more closely. Rounding hides the scatter rather than reducing it, and a single trial gives no measure of precision at all.

questions.stem: A force of 2.4 N acts through a distance of 0.135 m. How should the work done be reported, to an appropriate number of significant figures?
questions.explanation: 2.4 × 0.135 = 0.324 J. The answer can have no more significant figures than the least precise data, 2.4 N, with two, so it is 0.32 J. Keeping three or four figures claims more precision than the force measurement has.

questions.stem: A pendulum’s period is T = 2π√(L/g). To find g, a student plots T² against the length L. What does the gradient of the line equal?
options: 2π/√g
4π²g
4π²/g
g/4π²
questions.explanation: Squaring T = 2π√(L/g) gives T² = (4π²/g)L, a straight line through the origin with gradient 4π²/g. So g = 4π²/gradient. Plotting T against L would give a curve, which is why the data are linearised.

questions.stem: For a pendulum, T = 2π√(L/g). A graph of T² against L has a gradient of 4.0 s² m⁻¹. What value of g does this give?
options: 160 m s⁻²
1.6 m s⁻²
9.9 m s⁻²
questions.explanation: The gradient equals 4π²/g, so g = 4π²/4.0 ≈ 39.5/4.0 ≈ 9.9 m s⁻². Multiplying the gradient by 4π² gives 160 m s⁻², and inverting the relationship gives 0.10 m s⁻².

questions.stem: A student measures the force F between two charged spheres at several separations r. Which graph should give a straight line through the origin if F ∝ 1/r²?
options: F against 1/r
F against 1/√r
F against 1/r²
F against r²
questions.explanation: If F = k/r², then plotting F against 1/r² linearises the data into a straight line through the origin, with gradient k. Plotting F against r², 1/r or 1/√r gives a curve. Choosing the axes so the expected relationship is linear makes it easy to test.

questions.stem: A student plots the length of a hanging spring (vertical axis) against the weight hung from it (horizontal axis). What does the vertical intercept represent?
options: The spring’s natural, unstretched length
The spring constant of the spring
The elastic potential energy it stores
The extension at the spring’s elastic limit
questions.explanation: The intercept is the value of the vertical variable when the horizontal one is zero, so it is the spring’s length with no weight hung on it. Extrapolating a graph back to an intercept often gives a quantity of physical significance like this.

questions.stem: A graph of a spring’s extension (vertical axis) against the applied force (horizontal axis) is a straight line with a gradient of 0.020 m N⁻¹. What is the spring constant?
options: 25 N m⁻¹
100 N m⁻¹
50 N m⁻¹
questions.explanation: Since x = F/k, the gradient of extension against force is 1/k, so k = 1/0.020 = 50 N m⁻¹. Reading the gradient directly as k ignores which variable is on which axis.

questions.stem: What do uncertainty bars on the points of a graph show?
options: The exact error between each point and the true value
Which of the points are outliers that should be removed from the data
The gradient of the line of best fit at each point
The range within which each measured value is likely to lie
questions.explanation: Uncertainty bars show the uncertainty in each measurement, the range in which its true value probably lies. A line of best fit that passes through all the bars is consistent with the data. They do not show the exact error, which is unknown if the true value is unknown.

questions.stem: A straight line through the origin passes within the uncertainty bars of every point on a graph. What can the student conclude?
options: The data contain no systematic errors of any kind
Every one of the measurements is perfectly accurate
The data are consistent with a directly proportional relationship
The relationship is proven to be exactly proportional in all cases
questions.explanation: A line through every uncertainty bar shows that the data are consistent with proportionality within experimental uncertainty. It cannot prove the relationship holds everywhere, and a systematic error could still shift all the points without changing the shape.

questions.stem: A graph of voltage against current for a resistor should pass through the origin, but the line of best fit has a vertical intercept of 0.20 V. What does this most likely indicate?
options: A systematic error, such as a voltmeter with a zero offset
A random error, because the points scatter about the line
That the resistor has a resistance of exactly 0.20 Ω
That the current is 0.20 A when the voltage is zero
questions.explanation: An offset that shifts every reading by the same amount moves the whole line up without changing its gradient, which is the signature of a systematic error such as a zero error. Random errors scatter points around the line rather than shifting it. Resistance is given by the gradient, not the intercept.

questions.stem: A student uses a low-power laser in a double slit experiment. Which is the most appropriate control in the risk assessment?
options: Check the beam’s alignment by looking at it in a mirror held at arm’s length
Keep the beam below eye level and never look along it or at its reflections
Wear sunglasses so that the laser beam can be viewed directly when needed
Do the experiment only in a brightly lit room, so the beam is less intense
questions.explanation: The main hazard is eye damage from the direct or reflected beam, so the control keeps the beam away from eyes. Sunglasses are not laser protection, and room lighting does not change the beam’s intensity. Looking at reflections is exactly the exposure to avoid.

questions.stem: A class will investigate transformers. Which practice is safest?
options: Hold the bare ends of the wires together to keep the connections steady
Leave the supply on while rewiring, so the changes can be seen as they happen
Use a low-voltage AC supply and switch off before changing any connections
Connect the primary coil directly to a 230 V wall socket for a larger output
questions.explanation: Low-voltage supplies reduce the risk of electric shock, and switching off before changing connections removes it while wires are handled. Mains voltage is never used for student-built circuits, and bare wires should never be held while live.

questions.stem: What information does a safety data sheet (SDS) provide?
options: The uncertainty in each measuring instrument used in an experiment
The hazards of a substance, how to handle it safely and first aid
The results that earlier experiments using a substance produced
The accepted values of physical constants needed for calculations
questions.explanation: A safety data sheet gives a substance’s hazards, safe handling and storage, protective equipment and first aid. Risk assessments for investigations draw on safety data sheets for any chemicals involved.

questions.stem: Which action is a breach of ethical conduct when reporting an investigation?
options: Stating the limitations of the method in the discussion
Leaving out results that do not support the hypothesis
Recording an outlier and explaining why it was excluded
Acknowledging a classmate who helped to collect data
questions.explanation: Selectively omitting results to make a hypothesis look supported misrepresents the evidence. Recording outliers with reasons, acknowledging help and stating limitations are all part of honest, ethical reporting.

questions.stem: A student plans to measure classmates’ reaction times by catching a dropped ruler. What is most important ethically?
options: Publishing each participant’s name alongside their own reaction time
Obtaining informed consent and keeping individual results confidential
Choosing only the fastest classmates, so the data look more consistent
Not telling the participants what is being measured until afterwards
questions.explanation: People taking part in an investigation must agree to it knowing what is involved, and their personal results should be kept confidential. Choosing only fast participants biases the sample, and publishing names breaches privacy.

questions.stem: Which statement is evidence rather than opinion?
options: Faster driving is probably more dangerous than slow driving in every case
Most people believe that heavier cars always stop more safely than light ones
This investigation was clearly the best designed of any in the whole class
The mean stopping distance rose from 12 m to 19 m as the speed increased
questions.explanation: Evidence is data or observations that others can check, such as measured stopping distances. A belief, a judgement or a claim about what most people think is opinion, however reasonable it sounds.

questions.stem: Which of these claims is scientific, in the sense that it can be tested by experiment?
options: A heavier pendulum bob gives a pendulum a longer period
Physics is the most beautiful of all the sciences to study
Pendulums are far more elegant than springs as oscillators
The greatest physicist ever was the one who explained gravity
questions.explanation: A scientific claim makes a prediction that measurements could support or refute. The pendulum claim is testable, and in fact experiments refute it, since the period does not depend on the mass. Claims about beauty, elegance or greatness are value judgements that no experiment can settle.

questions.stem: A hypothesis states that the induced emf is proportional to the number of turns on a coil. The results are 0.52 V for 100 turns, 1.01 V for 200 turns and 1.55 V for 300 turns, each ± 0.05 V. What should the student conclude?
options: The data support the hypothesis only for the coil with 300 turns
The data support the hypothesis, as emf is proportional to turns within the uncertainty
The data refute the hypothesis, because 1.01 V is not exactly double 0.52 V
The data prove the hypothesis is true for every possible coil and magnet
questions.explanation: Proportionality predicts about 0.52 V, 1.04 V and 1.56 V, and every result lies within ± 0.05 V of these. So the data support the hypothesis within experimental uncertainty. Small differences inside the uncertainty do not refute it, and three points cannot prove it for every case.

questions.stem: From tests at speeds of 2 to 6 m s⁻¹, a student concludes that the drag force on a model car is proportional to its speed. What is a limitation of this conclusion?
options: The conclusion is wrong unless every point lies exactly on the line
The relationship may not hold outside the range of speeds tested
Five data points prove the relationship for all shapes and sizes
Proportional data means the drag is independent of the car’s shape
questions.explanation: A conclusion is only supported within the range of conditions tested. Drag often depends more strongly on speed at higher speeds, so extrapolating beyond 6 m s⁻¹ is not justified by this data. Points need to lie within their uncertainties of the line, not exactly on it.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of drawing a field as a set of field lines?
options: It shows the field only along the drawn lines, though it exists everywhere in the region
It shows the exact paths that charged particles always follow through the field
It allows field lines to cross wherever the fields of two sources happen to meet
It can only be used for gravitational fields, not for electric or magnetic fields
questions.explanation: Field lines are a model: their direction shows the force direction and their spacing the strength, but the field also exists between the lines drawn. Lines never cross, and the model works for all three fields. Charged particles do not in general follow field lines.

questions.stem: Newton’s laws of motion are a model of motion. What is their main limitation?
options: They cannot predict the motion of projectiles launched close to Earth’s surface
They apply only to objects that are at rest, not to moving objects
They have been replaced entirely and are no longer used by physicists
They give wrong predictions for objects moving close to the speed of light
questions.explanation: Newton’s laws are very accurate at everyday speeds and are still used in engineering and spaceflight. Near the speed of light their predictions fail, and special relativity is needed. Every model has a range of conditions in which it is valid.

questions.stem: Why does a student keep a logbook during a VCE physics investigation?
options: To present the final results to a non-technical audience in a short form
To store only the final, corrected data set once the analysis is complete
To replace the risk assessment that would otherwise have to be written
To authenticate their own primary data and record any changes to the method
questions.explanation: The logbook is a dated, ongoing record of planning, raw data, observations and changes to the method, which authenticates the work as the student’s own. Final results for an audience go on the poster, and the logbook must keep raw data, not just corrected values.

questions.stem: Which content belongs in the discussion section of a scientific poster?
options: A list of the equipment used and each of the method’s steps in numbered order
The raw data table exactly as recorded, before any processing was done
The research question and the hypothesis that the investigation tested
Evaluation of the method, including its limitations and sources of error
questions.explanation: The discussion interprets and evaluates the results: their link to physics concepts, limitations, sources of error and uncertainty, and implications. The method belongs in its own section, and the question and hypothesis come in the introduction.

questions.stem: A student’s poster includes a graph taken from a published article. What must the student do?
options: Redraw the graph so that no reference is then needed
Leave it out, since a poster may show only primary data
Label the graph as the student’s own primary data
Acknowledge the graph with a reference to its source
questions.explanation: Any information, data or image from another source must be acknowledged using a standard referencing convention. Redrawing someone else’s data does not make it the student’s own, and presenting it as primary data would be dishonest. Secondary data can support the discussion if it is referenced.

questions.stem: A student records a time of 0.000 45 s. Which shows this correctly in scientific notation and with a standard prefix?
options: 4.5 × 10⁴ s, or 45 ks
questions.explanation: 0.000 45 s = 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ s, and since 1 ms = 10⁻³ s, this is 0.45 ms (or 450 µs). Miscounting the decimal places gives 4.5 × 10⁻⁵ s or 4.5 × 10⁻³ s.

questions.stem: Which follows the conventions for drawing a results graph?
options: Independent variable on the horizontal axis, with each axis labelled with quantity and unit
Dependent variable on the horizontal axis, with units given only in the graph’s title
Independent variable on the vertical axis, with each point joined dot to dot
Either variable on either axis, provided all the points are joined by a curve
questions.explanation: By convention the independent variable goes on the horizontal axis and the dependent variable on the vertical axis, and each axis is labelled with the quantity and its unit. A line or curve of best fit is drawn rather than joining the points dot to dot.
